16050: Nebuchadnezzar II's blue glazed-brick gate, dedicated to Ishtar, decorated with bulls and dragons, with a long inscription. It stood at the head of the Processional Way during the years when Judean exiles lived in Babylon.
16054: Tablets of the descent myth show how the goddess and her lover were linked to death and return, the background to the Tammuz rite of Ezek 8.
16056: acquired by the British Museum 2003; known since 1930s
16058: A clay plaque (c. 1800 BC) of a winged, bird-footed goddess with lions and owls. It is often popularly labelled 'Lilith', but most specialists identify her as Ishtar or her sister Ereshkigal.
16060: Esth 2:7 says Hadassah was also called Esther. Many scholars derive Esther from Ishtar, as Mordecai is derived from Marduk; others prefer the Persian word for 'star'. This is not a hostile renaming but a court name.
16061: Ishtar's worship lasted in Mesopotamia into the Parthian period, and she merged with Aphrodite, Atargatis and other goddesses in the Greco-Roman East. Her descent myth has been widely studied as one of the earliest stories of death and return, though scholars now caution against the older idea of a single 'dying and rising god' pattern.
16072: A crescent moon, often a crescent on a pole with tassels; sometimes a bull with crescent horns
16073: Ehulhul temple, Harran (also the Ekishnugal temple at Ur)
16077: Sin was the moon god of Mesopotamia. His two great temples were at Ur in the south and Harran in the north — the two cities where Abraham's family lived. The Bible never names Sin, but it remembers that Abraham's ancestors 'served other gods' and repeatedly forbids worship of the moon.
16078: Sin was the wise, slow-moving father of the bright gods: the sun (Shamash) and Venus (Ishtar). He sailed across the night sky in a boat shaped like the crescent moon. Because the moon marks out months, he was the keeper of the calendar and the god who decided the timing of things. In one story, an eclipse is explained as demons attacking Sin, and the gods have to rescue him. Shepherds and cattle-herders were especially devoted to him, and he was believed to give oracles in dreams.
16079:
Abraham's father Terah moved the family from 'Ur of the Chaldees' to Harran (Gen 11:31). Both cities were famous centres of the moon god, and Josh 24:2 says plainly that Terah and his family 'served other gods' beyond the River. Some scholars note that family names like Laban ('white', a poetic word for the moon in Hebrew is levanah) and Milcah and Sarah (which resemble Malkatu and Sharratu, titles of moon-related goddesses at Harran) may echo moon worship. These name links are speculative but often discussed.

The Law forbids worship of 'the sun, or the moon, or the stars, all the host of heaven' (Deut 4:19; Deut 17:3), and Job lists kissing one's hand to the moon as a secret disloyalty to God (Job 31:26-28). Josiah later removed priests who burned incense to the moon (2 Kgs 23:5). By contrast, Gen 1:16 refuses even to name the sun and moon, calling them only 'the greater light' and 'the lesser light' — lamps made by God, not gods.

The last king of Babylon, Nabonidus, was a passionate devotee of Sin, which angered Marduk's priests. His son Belshazzar governed Babylon in his absence — which explains why Belshazzar can only offer Daniel the third place in the kingdom (Dan 5:7; Dan 5:29).
16080: Abraham's family leaves Ur for Harran
16081: The call of Abraham takes him out of two moon-god cities. Joshua's covenant speech later reminds Israel that its ancestors worshipped other gods there and calls them to choose (Josh 24:14-15).
16083: The sun, moon and stars are created things, not gods. Jeremiah pictures the bones of Jerusalem's leaders spread out before the sun and moon they served — the sky-gods watching, unable to help.
16085: Josiah's reform deposes the priests who burned incense 'to Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets'.
16087: Sennacherib's envoys boast that the gods of Harran could not save it from Assyria. Ezekiel later lists Harran as one of Tyre's trading partners.
16089: Cuneiform texts show Belshazzar was regent for his father Nabonidus, who spent years in Arabia and promoted Sin; Daniel's 'third ruler' detail fits this arrangement.
16090: Harran stelae of Nabonidus and Adad-guppi
16092: Harran, south-east Turkey (reused as paving in the Great Mosque)
16093: Inscriptions of Nabonidus and his mother Adad-guppi, a devotee of Sin who claimed to have lived over 100 years. They describe Sin's anger, the god's ten-year abandonment of Harran, and Nabonidus's rebuilding of the Ehulhul temple. They show the king's devotion to the moon god that so annoyed Babylon's priests.
16096: Nabonidus prays to Sin for himself and for 'Belshazzar, my firstborn son'. This was one of the first texts to confirm Belshazzar as a historical figure, whom some nineteenth-century critics had doubted.
16097: Ziggurat and temple of Nanna at Ur
16100: Woolley excavated the great moon-god ziggurat and residences of the high priestesses of Nanna, including those of Ennigaldi-Nanna, Nabonidus's daughter. Whether biblical 'Ur of the Chaldees' is this southern Ur or a northern site near Harran is debated, though southern Ur is the majority view.
16101: Moon-god stelae at Hazor and Bethsaida
16104: A Late Bronze Age shrine at Hazor had a stele with two raised hands beneath a crescent; an Iron Age stele at Bethsaida's city gate shows a bull-headed figure with a crescent, a type found in Aram. They show moon worship in the land itself.
16105: Harran's moon cult outlived almost every other Mesopotamian religion. The Roman emperor Caracalla was murdered in AD 217 on his way to the moon temple; the emperor Julian sacrificed there in 363. Pagans of Harran, called 'Sabians' by Muslim writers, kept the cult alive until the eleventh century. The popular claim that Islam's crescent or Allah derives from the moon god Sin is not supported by historians: the crescent became an Islamic emblem only centuries later under Ottoman influence.
16115: A star (the 'star of your god', Amos 5:26)
16116: Mesopotamian astral cult (no single temple; shown at Babylon)
16117: Sakkuth and Kaiwan are two star-gods mentioned once by Amos, who accuses Israel of carrying their images. Kaiwan is the Mesopotamian name for the planet Saturn. Stephen quotes the same verse in Acts from the Greek translation, where the name has become 'Rephan'.
16118: There is no story about these gods. Kayamanu, 'the steady one', was the Babylonian name for Saturn, the slowest of the visible planets. Sakkut appears in Mesopotamian lists of gods and is connected with Ninurta, a warrior god, who was also linked to Saturn. In the Babylonian incantation series *Shurpu*, Sakkut and Kayamanu are listed side by side, which explains why Amos pairs them.
16119:
Amos asks whether Israel offered sacrifices in the wilderness, then says, 'You shall take up Sikkuth your king and Kiyyun your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves' (Amos 5:26, in a literal rendering). Older translations such as the KJV read the words as common nouns: 'the tabernacle (sukkat) of your Moloch and Chiun'. Modern scholars mostly read them as divine names because of the Mesopotamian pair.

A debate surrounds the verb tense: is Amos describing idolatry in the wilderness, idolatry in his own day (8th century BC, when Assyrian astral influence was growing), or what Israel will carry into exile (Amos 5:27)? Scholars differ.

Stephen quotes the passage in Acts 7:42-43 from the Septuagint: 'you took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan'. The Greek translators read Hebrew *kiyyun* as something like *raiphan* — most likely an ancient copying confusion between similar letters, perhaps influenced by an Egyptian name for Saturn. Stephen uses the verse to argue that Israel's idolatry began in the wilderness right after the golden calf (Acts 7:41).
16121: Amos uses the star-gods to show that Israel's worship had been compromised, and threatens exile 'beyond Damascus'.
16122: Stephen: the star of your god Rephan
16123: Stephen's speech links the golden calf, the host of heaven, Moloch and Rephan into one story of rejection, quoting the Greek text of Amos.
16124: Worship of the host of heaven
16125: Kings records that both northern Israel and later Manasseh of Judah worshipped 'all the host of heaven', the wider astral religion to which Sakkuth and Kaiwan belong.
16127: edited by Erica Reiner, 1958 (tablets from Nineveh and elsewhere)
16128: Library of Ashurbanipal and other Mesopotamian archives
16129: This exorcism series lists the gods Sakkut and Kayamanu next to each other, the same pairing found in Amos 5:26. This is the main reason scholars read Amos's words as divine names.
16132: Records of planetary observations name Saturn as kayamanu, confirming the planetary meaning of Kaiwan.
16134: The Hebrew vowels of both names (i-u) appear to copy the vowels of *shiqquts*, 'detestable thing', a word used for idols — the same scribal technique that turned Ashtart into Ashtoreth. The Greek form Rephan probably arose from misreading the Hebrew letters.
16135: The names vanished from worship but survive in Bible translations, where they have caused centuries of confusion. Because Acts 7:43 calls Rephan's symbol a 'star', some modern groups have claimed that the six-pointed Star of David derives from 'the star of Remphan'. Historians reject this: the hexagram became a Jewish emblem only in the Middle Ages and has no connection with Amos's star-god.
16140: unknown — named only as the god in whose temple Sennacherib was killed
16141: Unknown; the popular eagle-headed image is a nineteenth-century misidentification
16143: Nisroch is the god in whose temple the Assyrian king Sennacherib was murdered by his own sons, after his failed siege of Jerusalem. No Assyrian god by this exact name is known, so scholars still argue over who he was. The murder itself is confirmed by Babylonian and Assyrian records.
16144: No myth survives because no god called Nisroch is attested outside the Bible. Proposed identifications include Nusku, the fire god and divine messenger, who had a temple at Nineveh; Ninurta, the warrior god; Ashur, the national god of Assyria (with the name garbled in copying); and Marduk. Each suggestion requires assuming that the Hebrew form has been altered, either accidentally or deliberately.
16145:
Kings and Isaiah tell the same story. Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC and mocked Hezekiah's trust in Yahweh. The angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib returned to Nineveh. 'And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword' (2 Kgs 19:37; Isa 37:38). His son Esarhaddon succeeded him.

The irony is deliberate. Sennacherib's envoys had asked, 'Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?' (2 Kgs 18:33). In the end Sennacherib's own god could not protect him in his own temple. The narrative compresses time: the murder happened in 681 BC, twenty years after the siege, which the text does not hide but does not stress either.
16146: Sennacherib killed in the house of Nisroch
16147: The king who mocked Israel's God is cut down by his sons while worshipping his own. Chronicles adds that he returned 'with shame of face'.
16149: The Rabshakeh's speech lists the gods of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivah, none of whom saved their people. The Nisroch scene answers this boast.
16151: acquired by the British Museum in the 1880s
16152: The chronicle records that on the 20th of Tebet (681 BC) 'his son killed Sennacherib, king of Assyria, in a rebellion', confirming the biblical account of a son's murder of the king.
16156: Esarhaddon describes how his brothers revolted, 'butting each other like young goats' for the kingship, and how he defeated them. In 1980 Simo Parpola argued from a letter that the murderer was Arda-Mulissu, which matches the biblical Adrammelech; this is widely accepted.
16157: Sennacherib's Prism (Taylor and Oriental Institute prisms)
16159: Sennacherib's own account of the 701 BC campaign says he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage', received heavy tribute, but conspicuously does not claim to have taken the city.
16160: Because the name is otherwise unknown, many scholars think it is a corrupted or deliberately distorted form of a known god's name. No consensus has emerged on which god.
16161: In 1849 Austen Henry Layard labelled the eagle-headed winged figures on Assyrian palace reliefs 'Nisroch', and the label stuck in popular books. Specialists now know those figures are apkallu, protective sages, not a god. Later demonologies made Nisroch a chief cook of hell, which is pure invention.
16167: child sacrifice by fire, according to 2 Kgs 17:31
16170: Adrammelech and Anammelech were the gods of Sepharvaim, whose people were resettled in Samaria by the Assyrians. The Bible says these settlers burned their children in the fire to them. Where Sepharvaim was, and who exactly these gods were, is still debated.
16171: No myths survive. The names look like compounds with -melek ('king'). Adrammelech has been read as Adad-milki ('Adad is king', Adad being the storm god, the Mesopotamian Hadad) or as a West Semitic Adar-malik ('the glorious one is king'). Anammelech may contain Anu, the sky god, or Anat. Because child sacrifice is not well attested in Mesopotamia proper, some scholars think Sepharvaim was a Syrian town where Levantine molk-type rites were practised.
16172:
The list of settlers' gods ends: 'the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim' (2 Kgs 17:31). The same city appears in the Assyrian boast — 'Where are the gods of Sepharvaim?' (2 Kgs 18:34; 2 Kgs 19:13). The writer of Kings uses these foreign gods to show how far the land had fallen: the territory of Israel, already condemned for passing children through the fire (2 Kgs 17:17), now hosts openly imported child sacrifice.

Confusingly, Adrammelech is also the name of one of Sennacherib's sons who murdered him (2 Kgs 19:37). The two are unrelated; the son's name has been matched with the Assyrian Arda-Mulissu.

**Where was Sepharvaim?** Options include Sippar in Babylonia (an old guess, now less favoured because the other places in the list are mostly Syrian), Sibraim between Damascus and Hamath (Ezek 47:16), or an otherwise unknown Syrian town. Debated.
16173: Settlers burn children to the gods of Sepharvaim
16174: The narrator lists this among the practices of the new population of Samaria, who 'feared the LORD' while serving their own gods.
16175: Where are the gods of Sepharvaim?
16176: Assyria's envoy cites Sepharvaim as a conquered city whose gods failed, to frighten Jerusalem into surrender.
16178: The law forbids making children 'pass through the fire', so the Sepharvite rite is presented as the climax of everything Israel had been warned against.
16179: Sargon II's deportation records (Nimrud Prism, Khorsabad annals)
16181: Assyrian texts describe moving conquered peoples into Samaria, the policy that brought the Sepharvites there. Sepharvaim itself has not been securely identified.
16182: The gods are known only from this passage. Milton placed Adramelec among the rebel angels in *Paradise Lost*, and later occult writers turned him into a demon of high rank — an invention with no ancient basis.
16186: uncertain; if Sarpanitu, pregnancy and birth, and consort of Marduk
16189: Succoth-benoth is the god or goddess that settlers from Babylon set up in Samaria. In Hebrew the name means 'booths of daughters', which sounds more like a place than a deity, so most scholars think it is a garbled or mocking form of a Babylonian name — most often Sarpanitu, Marduk's wife.
16190: If Succoth-benoth is Sarpanitu, she was the consort of Marduk, honoured alongside him in the Esagila temple, and associated with pregnancy and birth. A popular etymology linked her name to *zer-banitu*, 'creatress of seed', which may explain how Hebrew ears heard -benoth. Other suggestions are Marduk himself (via an epithet) or Banitu, 'creatress', a title of several goddesses.
16191:
'The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth' (2 Kgs 17:30). Since every other group in the list makes a god, Succoth-benoth must be the deity of the Babylonian settlers, which points to Marduk or his consort.

An older interpretation, found in some nineteenth-century commentaries, took the Hebrew literally as 'booths of daughters' and connected it with Herodotus's story (*Histories* 1.199) of Babylonian women sitting in a temple precinct until a stranger paid for sex. Most modern scholars reject both the literal reading of the name and the reliability of Herodotus's account of 'sacred prostitution'.
16192: The men of Babylon make Succoth-benoth
16193: The Babylonian settlers set up their own deity in Samaria's high places.
16196: Royal inscriptions and temple rituals name Sarpanitu as Marduk's consort in the Esagila. These support, but do not prove, the identification with Succoth-benoth.
16198: The Hebrew may reflect what a foreign name sounded like to Hebrew speakers, or a deliberate reshaping into a mildly mocking phrase. The exact mechanism is unknown.
16199: Known only from 2 Kgs 17:30. Milton does not list her, but some later demonologies made Succorbenoth a demon of jealousy, without any ancient basis.
16204: uncertain; possibly a divine 'Name' or hypostasis
16206: Ashima was the god of the settlers from Hamath in Syria who were moved into Samaria. Almost nothing is known about this deity. The name may also lie behind Amos's phrase 'the sin of Samaria', and a similar divine name appears among the Jewish soldiers at Elephantine in Egypt.
16207: No myths survive. Hamath was an Aramean and Neo-Hittite city on the Orontes river, conquered by Assyria in 720 BC. The best extra-biblical parallel is the name Eshem-Bethel or Ashim-Bethel in a fifth-century BC list of temple contributions from Elephantine, which may mean 'the Name of Bethel' — a divine aspect worshipped alongside the god Bethel.
16208: 'The men of Hamath made Ashima' (2 Kgs 17:30). Amos, preaching decades earlier, condemns those 'who swear by the sin of Samaria' (Amos 8:14). The Hebrew for 'sin' is *ashmat*, and many scholars think Amos is punning on, or directly naming, a goddess Ashimah worshipped in Samaria; others take it simply as 'guilt' or as a reference to the calf at Bethel. If the first view is right, Ashima was in Samaria before the deportations, which complicates 2 Kgs 17:30. Debated.
16209: The men of Hamath make Ashima
16210: Hamathite settlers bring their deity into the high places of the former northern kingdom.
16211: Swearing by the guilt of Samaria
16212: Amos lists oaths by 'the sin of Samaria', 'your god, O Dan', and 'the way of Beersheba'. The first may be a pun on Ashima.
16216: A fifth-century BC Aramaic list of donations for 'Yahu' also sets aside money for Eshem-Bethel and Anat-Bethel. It shows a Jewish colony honouring other divine names, and gives the closest known parallel to Ashima.
16219: Excavations uncovered the Iron Age citadel of Hamath, destroyed by Sargon II in 720 BC, but no inscription naming Ashima.
16220: Ashmat Shomron, 'the guilt of Samaria' (Amos 8:14), if a pun
16221: Changing one sound turns the deity's name into the Hebrew word for 'guilt', a technique seen elsewhere in the Bible's treatment of foreign gods. The pun is plausible but not certain.
16222: Known only from these verses and the Elephantine parallel. The Talmud (b. Sanhedrin 63b) says Ashima had the form of a goat, a rabbinic tradition with no known ancient support.
16228: Unknown (rabbinic tradition says Nibhaz was dog-shaped and Tartak donkey-shaped)
16229: Samaria, where the Avvites set them up (Avva itself is unlocated)
16230: Nibhaz and Tartak were the gods of the Avvites, one of the groups Assyria resettled in Samaria. They are the least understood gods in the Bible: we do not know where Avva was or what these gods were like.
16231: No myths or inscriptions are known. Scholars have offered guesses: an Elamite origin (from south-west Iran), a link between Tartak and the Syrian goddess Atargatis, or an Aramaic origin. None has won general support.
16232: 'The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak' (2 Kgs 17:31). Avva is probably the same as Ivvah, one of the cities whose gods failed to stop Assyria (2 Kgs 18:34; 2 Kgs 19:13). The passage's point is cumulative: one group after another brings its own god into the land, while also learning to 'fear the LORD', so that 'unto this day' they do both (2 Kgs 17:41).
16233: The Avvites make Nibhaz and Tartak
16234: The last of the imported gods in the list of settlers' deities.
16236: The narrator concludes that these nations feared the LORD and served their graven images at the same time, a pattern he condemns.
16238: Assyrian royal inscriptions confirm the two-way deportations that brought foreign groups into Samaria. No text mentions Nibhaz or Tartak.
16239: Rabbinic tradition (b. Sanhedrin 63b) explains Nibhaz as a dog ('barker', from *nabah*) and Tartak as a donkey, guesses based on Hebrew wordplay. Medieval demonologies later made Nibhaz a demon. Nothing more is known.
16244: The shepherd's crook and flocks; reed huts and sheepfolds
16245: Uruk and Bad-tibira (southern Iraq); shown at Uruk
16247: Tammuz (Sumerian Dumuzi) was a shepherd god, the lover of the goddess Ishtar, who was taken down to the underworld. Each year women mourned his death in the summer heat. Ezekiel saw women of Jerusalem 'weeping for Tammuz' at the very gate of God's temple.
